DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekly Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

**The pilot is a genuine strength, and the cost table adds up. But the study's own data contradict two of its central claims, and correcting them changes the conclusion.**

- **Flats.** Participation in flats was a third of the level in houses, not "broadly similar."
- **Tonnage.** The projection uses a participation rate that doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot results.
- **Brookfield's capacity.** Brookfield can take only about 60% of the projected tonnage, which the financial analysis ignores.

Corrected, the net cost exceeds the provisional funding, and "fully funded" no longer holds.

## 1. Participation was not similar across housing types

Table 1 shows **66% participation in houses and 21% in flats**. On the measure the study itself uses, flats participated at **about a third** of the rate of houses. The text's claim that participation "was broadly similar across housing types," and the conclusion that the service can be "rolled out uniformly," contradict the table directly.

Flats make up about 20% of the district, roughly 10,400 households. Their low uptake is common in food waste schemes and usually calls for a different service: communal bins, different collection points, and targeted communications. This finding should change the recommendation, not just the wording.

## 2. The tonnage projection uses an unexplained rate

- **The rate used.** Section 3 applies "the pilot's **64%** participation rate." But the pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and no figure in the pilot is 64%.
- **The pilot's mix matches the district.** The pilot was 20% flats, and so is the district. That makes 57% the directly comparable rate. Better still, the projection should be calculated separately for each housing type.

**Corrected projection:**

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | about 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | about 159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **about 2,870** |

That is about **13% lower** than the 3,290 tonnes in the study. The study's own calculation is arithmetically correct (52,000 × 0.64 × 1.9 × 52 ≈ 3,290); the problem is the 64% input.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

Brookfield offers **1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. The projection is about 2,870 tonnes, or 3,290 on the study's own figures. That leaves **about 1,070 to 1,490 tonnes a year without a destination** for at least the first two years.

The study mentions this capacity limit, then calculates the full saving as if every tonne went to Brookfield. It never discusses the shortfall. The author's summary that "treatment is local" is therefore only partly true. The excess would need to go to the plant 46 miles away, which brings:
- **an unknown gate fee**,
- **extra haulage:** a 92-mile round trip, more vehicle and crew time, possibly a transfer arrangement,
- or the food waste being collected and then incinerated anyway.

None of these costs appears in the study.

## 4. The effect on the finances

The cost table is correct:
- Vehicles: 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 years = £141,400
- Crews: 6 crews of 2 × £34,000 = £408,000
- Total: £733,400

The savings line is the problem.

| Scenario | Disposal saving | Net cost | vs £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Study as written: 3,290 t, all at Brookfield | £243,000 | **£490,000** | £30,000 headroom |
| Corrected tonnage: 2,870 t, all at Brookfield | about £212,500 | **about £521,000** | **about £1,000 over** |
| Corrected, Brookfield capped at 1,800 t | £133,200 at Brookfield, plus an unknown amount for the excess | **up to about £600,000** | **up to about £80,000 over**, less any net saving on the excess |

The last row assumes the excess saves nothing. If the 46-mile plant's gate fee plus haulage comes in under £112 a tonne, some saving remains. But that figure needs to be found out, not assumed.

**Even on the study's own figures, the headroom is only £30,000, about 6%.** And the funding itself is uncertain: the Government has "indicated" funding, and the allocation is "provisional." The study should not describe the service as "fully funded" until the allocation is confirmed.

## 5. Costs that are missing

The author calls the analysis "complete," but the following costs are absent or unclear:

- **Relief cover** for holidays and sickness. Six crews of two with no spare capacity can't run reliably every week.
- **A spare vehicle**, for breakdowns and servicing.
- **Supervision, round planning and management time.**
- **Recruitment and training**, which the timetable requires.
- **Haulage and disposal of tonnage beyond Brookfield's capacity.**
- **The dedicated phone line and web page.** These may be included under "communications," but the study doesn't say.
- **Financing costs** on the vehicle purchase, if they're borrowed or leased.

Each of these widens the gap between the net cost and the funding.

## 6. Limits of the pilot evidence

- **The season.** The pilot ran from January to June. Food waste yields and participation vary through the year, and summer and autumn aren't covered.
- **Novelty.** Participation often falls after the launch period. Six months may not show the long-term rate.
- **The survey.** The 81% satisfaction figure is from "surveyed" households, but the response rate isn't given, and keen participants may be over-represented. It's encouraging, but it shouldn't be treated as representative.
- **Weekly data.** The author says the pilot measured participation and tonnage weekly, but the study reports only six-month averages. Showing the weekly trend would let the Council see whether participation held up or was declining.

## 7. What's sound

- The pilot design: a real local trial, deliberately mixed wards, results by housing type, and contamination spot-checked at the plant.
- Low contamination (under 2%) and steadily falling missed-collection reports.
- The cost arithmetic, the £74 per tonne disposal differential and its calculation.
- A clear implementation timetable worked back from the vehicle lead time. Recruiting crews from February and training them in March is tight, though, and the December order date depends on Cabinet deciding quickly.

## Recommended changes before this goes to Cabinet

1. **Correct the description of flats** and set out a specific approach for them, with its cost.
2. **Recalculate tonnage by housing type**, giving about 2,870 tonnes, or explain where 64% came from.
3. **Address Brookfield's capacity limit.** Get a gate fee and haulage cost from the 46-mile plant, or another option, for the excess tonnage until 2029, and include it in the finances.
4. **Add the missing cost lines**, especially relief cover, a spare vehicle and supervision.
5. **Present the funding position honestly.** On corrected figures, the net cost roughly equals or exceeds the provisional allocation, and the allocation isn't confirmed. Include a funding-gap scenario and say how any gap would be met.
6. **Show the weekly pilot trend** and the survey response rate.

The service is a statutory requirement, so the question is how to deliver it rather than whether to. Cabinet should approve it knowing the actual funding risk, not on the basis that it's fully funded.
